canberra.title: Scared about making a change in your life? Jessica Mauboy is right there with you
canberra.snippet: Spending 20 years in the spotlight would make award-winning singer, songwriter and actress Jessica Mauboy comfortable with curve balls an...
canberra.content:
Jessica Mauboy will be in Canberra for one night only on 3 October. Photo: Higher Press/Supplied.

Spending 20 years in the spotlight would make award-winning singer, songwriter and actress Jessica Mauboy comfortable with curve balls and change, right?

Nope.

“This is so completely out of my comfort zone, out of my world,” Jess told Region.

She’s talking about her one-night-only performance of The Story of Me: A Musical Journey Through My Career, coming to Canberra on 3 October.

It’s an exploration of her career from the first moment she stepped on the Australian Idol stage to breaking up with record labels and going it alone.

“This show scares me … it’s the most vulnerable and intimate I’ve ever been,” Jess said.

“But it also makes me feel liberated and know I can have a good, trusting yarn [with the audience] … we can trust in the process together.

“And also have a party by the end of it – get up and have a good sing and a shout.”

Australians may feel they know the girl from Darwin. Familiarity with a person’s image can create a sense of being part of their journey.

For Jess, the “nice girl” assumption is one that has followed her around for her entire career.

While it’s not entirely inaccurate, it’s not the full picture.

“I tend to get that a lot: ‘she’s a nice gal’,” Jess reflected.

“‘Nice’ is very classic, but that can mean anything … I’ve been in the public eye for a very long time, I look at all my chapters and I keep evolving.

“The nice girl can also be misunderstood.”

The Story of Me will examine Jess’s highs and lows, how she went from running barefoot in the dust to the very fast machine that is the music industry.

She’ll share her doubts about whether she could belong in show business, how she juggled staying authentic and honing her instincts while also needing to be aware of her business and brand.

Plus the fear and exhilaration that comes when you discover you need to take a leap of faith.

“At some point in our lives we all go: I need to change,” Jess said.

“Life gives you experiences or opportunities where we can remain comfortable and let the cycle continue. Or life gives you another door where things will be more challenging … where you have to trust yourself.

“I realised that trusting myself, trusting my stories meant more to me than I thought … and now, if I fall, that’ll be on me. And that’s okay.”

Audience members will experience heartfelt ballads, re-imagined classics and Jessica Mauboy’s signature powerhouse anthems.

You’ll leave knowing her “little secrets” and how different it is to step out and form an independent label.

You might also hear how it’s transformed her music.

“[I’ve been told] ‘you seem a little bit more like yourself’,” Jess said.

“I’m already working on my seventh studio album … this body of work – it’s the Jess that we know, but I think [people will also go] ‘I didn’t know she had that in her’.

“[I’ve found] when I feel a little bit scared of something, that’s good, for me … it make me my truest.”

She hopes the audience leaves inspired to appreciate the people in their lives, knowing they can be relied upon if that leap of faith needs to be taken.

“I hope I’m that person filling that cup for someone … that they can leave [the performance] feeling that they’re proud of themselves, that they’re confident and know what they’re doing,” Jess said.

“Change always comes, and I’m ready for it … this is the most solid I’ve ever felt in my life.”

Jessica Mauboy’s ‘The Story of Me: A Musical Journey Through My Career’, is on at the Canberra Theatre Centre on 3 October. Tickets are on sale now.

canberra.title: Endometriosis hospitalisations surge as Canberra patients face barriers to care
canberra.snippet: More Australian women and girls are ending up in hospital with endometriosis, but for those living in Canberra, getting the right diagnos...
canberra.content:
Young woman. Part of ‘Life with Endometriosis’ art photography project. Image by Margaret Kalms, used with permission.

More Australian women and girls are ending up in hospital with endometriosis, but for those living in Canberra, getting the right diagnosis and treatment can come with another hurdle: finding specialist care close to home.

Endometriosis is a chronic condition where tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, often causing severe pelvic pain and, for some, fertility problems.

New Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) data shows the rate of hospitalisation for endometriosis has jumped 23 per cent over the past decade, far outstripping the 5 per cent increase in hospitalisations among females overall.

There were 24,700 endometriosis hospitalisations across Australia in 2024-25, with more than nine in 10 involving a procedure. Seven in 10 admissions were in private hospitals.

AIHW spokesperson Amy Young said the condition could have a significant impact on people’s everyday lives.

“Endometriosis is a chronic condition that affects many Australian girls, women and people assigned female at birth, and can have a significant impact on their daily lives and overall wellbeing,” she said.

The figures come as the ACT Legislative Assembly initiated an inquiry to examine endometriosis and other pelvic pain conditions, with submissions to the inquiry in April arguing that some of the problems being seen nationally are compounded in Canberra by the size and structure of the territory’s health system.

The Health Care Consumers’ Association (HCCA) said ACT patients faced many of the same problems reported elsewhere in Australia – including delayed diagnosis, gender bias and fragmented pathways through the health system.

But it said Canberra patients could face additional difficulties due to reduced access to local specialists, higher costs and increased reliance on travelling interstate for care.

The organisation has called for a coordinated ACT response, including an integrated, publicly funded women’s health system covering everything from early identification and community assessment through to specialist and multidisciplinary hospital treatment.

Among its recommendations are longer funded GP consultations for complex pelvic pain, more gynaecologists, pain specialists and pelvic health physiotherapists, increased public surgical capacity and better access to advanced diagnostic imaging in Canberra.

It also wants changes to the Interstate Patient Travel Assistance Scheme to make it easier for patients forced to seek treatment outside the ACT.

When contacted by Region, the ACT Government said information about endometriosis and pelvic pain was being considered through the Assembly inquiry.

However, exactly how many Canberra patients are waiting for endometriosis surgery is not known. Canberra Health Services reports elective surgery waiting lists by clinical specialty rather than individual conditions.

A Canberra Health Services spokesperson said the health service recognised the “significant impact” endometriosis and chronic pelvic pain could have and had been strengthening its approach to treatment.

People referred for pelvic pain currently join a single gynaecology waiting list, with referrals reviewed by a specialist to determine the appropriate treatment.

Since July 2025, CHS has also operated an Endometriosis Pelvic Pain pathway aimed at getting patients assessed earlier and coordinating different parts of their care.

Depending on individual needs, patients can be referred to nursing, physiotherapy, psychology, pain management, allied health or specialist medical services.

CHS said it had also increased specialised nursing, physiotherapy and psychology support and would continue evaluating the pathway.

The pressure being examined in Canberra sits within a much larger national shift in how endometriosis is treated.

Almost two-thirds – 62 per cent – of endometriosis hospitalisations in 2024-25 involved laparoscopic excision or ablation, compared with 58 per cent a decade earlier.

The rate of laparoscopic excision rose substantially, from 57 to 93 hospitalisations per 100,000 females over the decade, while the rate of diathermy procedures declined.

Hormonal treatments, including the contraceptive pill and intrauterine devices, are recommended as first-line treatment for people who are not trying to conceive.

Hospital IUD insertions for endometriosis increased from 19 to 29 per 100,000 females over the decade.

“This aligns with clinical guidelines which recommend the use of hormonal treatments after laparoscopic surgery to help reduce the recurrence of symptoms,” Ms Young said.

But the national figures also reveal a substantial number of patients are still undergoing major surgery.

There were 3200 hysterectomies associated with endometriosis in 2024-25. More than nine in 10 were performed on women aged over 35, while fewer than 10 a year involved patients under 25.

The rate of abdominal hysterectomy for endometriosis has doubled over the past decade, from 11 to 23 procedures per 100,000 females.

Cost is another part of the problem.

Sexual Health Advocates for Reproductive Equity (SHARE), a group of young Australians campaigning for free access to contraception, told the ACT inquiry that financial barriers could restrict treatment choices for people managing endometriosis and pelvic pain.

Its national survey found two in five respondents said cost had limited their contraceptive choices, while more than one in three could not afford their preferred method. The group cited research estimating the lifetime burden of endometriosis at almost $130,000 per person, excluding associated conditions.

For HCCA, improving care in Canberra therefore requires more than simply increasing the number of procedures performed.

It wants earlier identification, clearer referral pathways, greater specialist capacity, better pain management, financial support and improved coordination between the different health professionals a patient may encounter.

It has also called for ACT-specific data on how long people wait for a diagnosis, how easily they can access treatment and their eventual health outcomes.

canberra.title: Market eats: 3 to try at the Old Bus Depot Markets
canberra.snippet: Through my various Canberra chapters, from uni student to suburban dweller and now someone who has swapped a house for inner-city apartme...
canberra.content:
Vitamin C in slushie form from Gourmet Scoops at Old Depot Markets. Photo: Sophia Brady.

Through my various Canberra chapters, from uni student to suburban dweller and now someone who has swapped a house for inner-city apartment living, some constants have remained. One of them is Sunday at the Old Bus Depot Markets.

Operating since 1994, the Kingston institution has become part of the rhythm of Canberra weekends.

Every Sunday, more than 200 stallholders fill the old industrial building with handcrafted wares, vintage treasures, jewellery, homewares, art and food.

A visit has invariably been a bit of a stamina game. With so many stalls spread throughout the market, there is always something to stop, look at, pick up, admire, or talk about with the person who made it.

Over the years, I have bought everything here from a Christmas tree to handcrafted spice mills, jewellery and art.

But part of the joy of any market visit is sustaining yourself along the way.

With stalls selling pastries, biscuits and all manner of sweet treats to take home, plus a busy food hall packed with cuisines from around the world, there is plenty to choose from. On a recent visit, I made these three stops.

Gourmet Scoops

Before tackling the serious business of market browsing, I needed something to drink.

The bright orange cups at Gourmet Scoops caught my eye. The stall continuously squeezes fresh oranges and, depending on the season, offers everything from large pots of warming mulled wine and teas to real fruit ice cream.

On a beautiful spring morning, there were plenty of choices, but I couldn’t pass up an orange juice slushie.

Sitting outside in the sunshine with my frozen, bright hit of vitamin C, watching the steady stream of market-goers wander past, life felt good. The frozen juice was refreshing, sweet and the perfect companion for a slow Sunday morning.

A colourful patchwork of flavours and aromas from Seni’s Ethiopian Cuisine. Photo: Sophia Brady.

Seni’s Ethiopian Cuisine

Tucked inside the food hall at the very back of the market, Seni’s Ethiopian Cuisine is one of those stalls that always seems to have a queue. Watching orders being assembled is almost as enjoyable as eating them.

Unable to decide between the seven curries on offer, I ordered the special, which includes a taste of everything served on injera, the traditional Ethiopian flatbread with its soft, spongy texture.

The preparation felt almost ceremonial. Each curry was carefully spooned onto the plate one by one, creating a colourful patchwork of flavours and aromas before being topped with another piece of injera.

The selection ranged from spicy beef to lentils and a pumpkin stew. I worked my way around the plate, trying to decide which curry was my favourite.

The injera on top is used to scoop up the curries, but the best bit comes at the end. The injera underneath absorbs all the juices and flavours from above, becoming a delicious reward after all the curries have disappeared.

Croffle – fun to say and to eat. Photo: Sophia Brady.

Croffle & Co

For dessert, I tried something entirely new to me. A croffle – fun to say and fun to eat. It combines the buttery layers of a croissant with the shape and crunch of a waffle.

At Croffle & Co, flavours include matcha chocolate, Nutella and Biscoff, and you can add toppings like fruit and candy.

For my first croffle experience, I kept things simple with cinnamon sugar.

At first glance, it looks like a waffle. Then you bite into it and discover the croissant layers hidden inside. Crisp on the outside, you get a pleasant crunch at first, followed by the buttery croissant layers underneath. The appeal is easy to see.

By the time I finished, market bags and tummy full, I was reminded why the Old Bus Depot Markets have remained a Canberra stalwart for more than three decades. There is always something new to discover, but there are also familiar favourites that keep people coming back Sunday after Sunday.

Visit the Old Bus Depot Markets at 21 Wentworth Ave, Kingston every Sunday from 9:30 am to 2:30 pm.

canberra.title: Canberra has plenty of empty car spaces. Bronte has an idea to put them to work
canberra.snippet: Every day, Bronte Hunter drove from a farm outside Canberra into Barton for work, and she handed over $16 just to leave her car somewhere...
canberra.content:
Parko works a little like Airbnb for parking – connecting people who have an empty car space with people looking for somewhere cheaper and more convenient to park. Photo: Region.

Every day, Bronte Hunter drove from a farm outside Canberra into Barton for work, and she handed over $16 just to leave her car somewhere.

With no public transport option, driving wasn’t really a choice. And for someone fresh out of university, the daily parking bill hurt.

Then she noticed something frustrating. The building where she worked had a large basement full of allocated parking spaces – and, by her estimate, it was regularly only about half full.

Some workers were paying around $8 a day to retain spaces they weren’t using, while Bronte was paying twice as much to park down the road.

“I was like, I would love to be able to use the parks in the building, so people that are paying for it and not using it … can get it back. And I can pay half price!” she said.

That frustration became Parko Services, a Canberra-built website that works a little like Airbnb for parking – connecting people who have an empty car space with people looking for somewhere cheaper and more convenient to park.

The concept is particularly suited to a city where many people still drive to work, but changing work patterns mean thousands of privately allocated spaces may not be used every day.

A public servant working from home two days a week could potentially rent their workplace space on those days. Someone living in an apartment in Civic or Woden could make their space available while they are at work. A resident going away for a fortnight could list theirs temporarily.

“How do we leverage this empty space so that people can have cheaper car parking, and the people who have the car parking have it as an income stream?” Bronte said.

And Canberrans appear interested.

Since launching in mid-May, Parko has attracted more than 5000 visits to its website, including almost 3000 in the previous 30 days. It has more than 20 hosts and 57 registered users, with spaces appearing around Civic, Woden, Barton, Manuka and Harrison near the light rail line.

Hosts decide when their space is available and set the price.

So far, Bronte said daily spaces are generally being offered for about $10, weekly spaces for $40 to $50 and monthly parking for around $150 to $200, depending on location.

The potential savings can be substantial.

Bronte points to Civic, where she said parking at the Canberra Olympic Pool costs $23 a day – $115 over a five-day working week. Parko hosts nearby are offering spaces for about $50 a week.

Some daily spaces are around $10, compared with early-bird commercial parking of about $20.

Parko Services founder Bronte Hunter created the platform after experiencing Canberra’s high parking costs herself. Photo: Supplied.

For Bronte, however, the longer-term opportunity is not simply cheaper parking. It is about making better use of parking Canberra has already built.

Hybrid working has changed the equation. Allocated office spaces can sit empty when employees work from home, while growing apartment precincts contain private spaces that may be unused for much of the day.

Parko is designed to allow those spaces to move in and out of the parking supply rather than requiring someone to rent them permanently.

Bronte first began developing the idea in 2024. When developers quoted around $60,000 to build the platform, she decided to teach herself how to do it.

“I could see the demand for it,” she said.

“Every person that I spoke to either would have been keen to use it, or keen to list a car space through it.”

“I decided I’d give it a try and learn how to build it myself.”

One of the bigger challenges will be getting Canberra’s apartment and commercial buildings involved.

Strata rules and building security can make sharing private parking more complicated, so Bronte has built a “communities” function that allows access to be restricted to particular residents or employees.

A building manager can approve users and see who is accessing its parking, while a workplace could restrict bookings to people with its company email address.

Bronte has begun speaking with strata companies and building managers and hopes eventually to approach property managers responsible for larger government buildings.

That could determine how far the idea ultimately goes.

Rather than creating more parking in areas where it is expensive or difficult to find, Parko’s proposition is that at least part of the answer could be hidden behind apartment gates and underneath office buildings – spaces that already exist but aren’t being used.

Bronte is still running Parko alongside another job and has delivered more than 12,000 flyers around Canberra herself, often spending evenings and weekends walking through areas where she thinks the concept could work.

Her goal is eventually to make the business her full-time job.

But her bigger ambition is for Parko to become something Canberrans automatically check before paying commercial parking rates.

“I would love it to become synonymous with Canberra parking,” she said.

To download Parko, scan the QR code.

Parko Services connects Canberrans looking for parking with people who have unused car spaces. Screenshot: Supplied.

canberra.title: Accidental discovery brings historic billiards table home to Braidwood
canberra.snippet: As a historic billiards table finds its way back home to a southern NSW town, there’s hope it can revitalise a new generation of pl...
canberra.content:
Before a billiards table can be moved, it needs to be disassembled – and that was how its Braidwood connection was found. Photo: John Stahel.

As a historic billiards table finds its way back home to a southern NSW town, there’s hope it can revitalise a new generation of players.

Braidwood Museum volunteer John Stahel is among a group who meet twice a week to play billiards. They’re following in the footsteps of previous generations – including those in 1894 who gathered to play.

“We’re probably a group of men – and it is mainly men – who, essentially, are doing exactly the same they were doing 125 years ago,” he said.

“We probably all sit there and talk about exactly the same rubbish about the drought or whatever it is.”

Purchasing the billiards table originally cost an estimated 87 pounds.

“They got that money back in about 18 months of renting it out, so it was obviously a very popular purchase,” John said.

The current group’s search began when the owner of their current table decided to sell it, meaning they couldn’t play in a private home any longer.

“It got us thinking – well, we’d better try and find another table somewhere.”

They collected one from the NSW Southern Highlands for $100.

Soon after, John said the club heard rumours another table was on the market. It led them to the Berowra RSL Club, which was seeking to offload a billiard table.

“We went, ‘Oh, well, we really don’t need another table but it’s free. We’re on a bit of a roll,” he said.

‘We know how to pull them apart and put them back together and everything.”

Coasters – also known as wafters – are often used to balance a billiards table. They’re normally hidden from view and only seen if a table needs to be repaired – or moved.

“As we were picking it up, we noticed that under one of the legs was a coaster, which was from the Braidwood Servicemen’s Club,” John said.

“A coaster underneath a billiard table is not something that just gets there accidentally – not with how heavy billiard tables are.”

John said research revealed that records from the Braidwood Literary Institute, compiled between the 1860s and the 1930s, recorded multiple billiard tables in their collection.

By the 1950s, one of the tables had been moved to the Braidwood Servicemen’s Club.

“We knew there was a good chance that this table had a real Braidwood connection,” John said.

“As we went through the records, we saw that it absolutely was [that table].”

The group is partnering with a Canberra-based company to handle the restoration.

John said, during their search, the group has been putting aside $10 each at their meetings.

“It’ll be completely restored. The reason the club at Berowra was getting rid of it, it was worn out.

“It’ll probably cost $5000 … and that [saved money] will go towards fixing the table.”

It’s expected the restoration will include polishing the frame, while the cushions and ball pockets will be replaced.

An exhibition space will also house it.

When that process is complete, John hopes billiards players will converge on the town.

“The club will book out the room twice a week at least, and then there’ll probably be a lot of people who are just casual players. We’ll certainly be encouraging visitors to play.

“It’s not going to be a huge money-spinner. We won’t be making a fortune out of it, but it will pay its way.”

australia.title: Alleged drone operator charged with murder after mistaken identity shooting in Sydney
australia.snippet: NSW police say 18-year-old was operating drone when arrested and likely ‘conducting surveillance on someone or some premises’ Get our bre...
australia.content:
A Sydney teenager has been charged with murder after police accused him of operating a drone as part of a suspected botched gang hit in the city’s west.

Joshua Macdonald, 40, was shot dead at a Merrylands West home on 2 September in what police believe may have been a case of mistaken identity. He was not known to police and had no links to organised crime.

His killing came a day after a seperate mistaken identity shooting in the city, which left 23-year-old university student, Marco Talia, dead in his Glen Alpine home.

NSW police on Friday arrested two men, aged 18 and 19. They alleged the younger man was involved in the killing of Macdonald.

“A drone was seized and forensically examined by detectives, who allegedly uncovered evidence to suggest involvement in the fatal shooting in Merrylands,” police said in a statement on Saturday.

The 18-year-old was charged with murder, participating in a criminal group and contributing to criminal activity and was expected to appear in bail court on Saturday.

The 19-year-old was charged with participating in a criminal group, contributing to criminal activity and driving with a suspended licence.

He was granted bail in Liverpool local court on Friday and was scheduled to return to court on 24 September.

NSW police said the 18-year-old was operating a drone when he was arrested on Friday morning.

“That behaviour is obviously of great concern to us,” Det Supt Joe Doueihi told reporters.

“It’s more than likely that he was involved in some type of criminality and conducting surveillance on someone or some premises. We are still in the process of identifying who that may have been.”

Doueihi alleged the teenager on 2 September was located a few blocks away from the house where Macdonald was killed and used the drone to surveil the area and pass information on to the shooters.

He was likely one of a number of people contracted by an organised crime group to carry out parts of the hit, the detective alleged.

Other roles contracted out for such a crime can include stealing a car or destroying evidence.

The shooting of Macdonald was at least the fifth suspected NSW mistaken identity killing since May 2025, with fears reckless overseas criminal leaders are ordering the attacks.

Senior NSW government ministers have insisted the situation was under control.

Last week, the acting NSW premier, Prue Car, said “police are on top of this”.

The police minister, Yasmin Catley, echoed that sentiment and said a new criminal model, which allegedly outsourced criminal activities to teenagers, was “very challenging”.

“Police are doing everything they can,” Catley said.

– with Australian Associated Press

australia.title: Court case brought by Zionist federation against journalist Mary Kostakidis ended ‘by consent’
australia.snippet: Former SBS newsreader had been accused by Zionist Federation of Australia of breaching Racial Discrimination Act when sharing X posts Get...
australia.content:
Federal court proceedings brought by the Zionist Federation of Australia (ZFA) against journalist Mary Kostakidis have been discontinued “by consent” with “no order as to costs”.

The former SBS newsreader had been accused by the federation of breaching the Racial Discrimination Act (RDA) by sharing two X posts about a speech by the late Hezbollah secretary general Hassan Nasrallah in January 2024.

Last year, Kostakidis had asked the court to strike the proceedings out, arguing the claim failed to identify which race, ethnicity or nationality was offended by her social media posts about Israel.

The chief executive of the ZFA, Alon Cassuto, had alleged the breach came when Kostakidis shared a video of a speech by Nasrallah on X and added: “The Israeli govt getting some of its own medicine. Israel has started something it can’t finish with this genocide.”

A second post sharing the same video was also part of the claim. The complaint was first raised with the Australian Human Rights Commission but escalated to the federal court.

The court said on Friday that the case had been dismissed with the agreement of both parties.

Kostakidis said in a statement she had spent “two years doing nothing but preparing my defence in a case aimed at silencing me” and the discontinuation was a “win for every Australian who values our democratic right to freedom of political expression”.

“I want to thank my fellow Australians who recognised the significance of what we stand to lose, stood with me and stepped up to assist me to launch my defence,” she said.

“The purpose of journalism is to get to the truth – fearlessly – and to hold power to account. This is a win for press freedom, which has prevailed.

“Watching a people livestream their own genocide while the international community responsible for creating this mess offers the victims sympathy and the perpetrators bombs, diplomatic cover and impunity, has been disgusting.”

In a statement published on Friday, Cassuto said his objectives in bringing the proceedings had been “substantially satisfied” after a public apology by Kostakidis in 2025 for the “hurt, distress and pain” felt by Jews and Israelis in Australia who took her posts “as an edorsement”.

“An important reason I brought this matter was to seek recognition of the harm these posts caused ordinary Jewish Australians,” he said.

“Given everything Ms Kostakidis has chosen to publish since her apology, a further apology compelled by a court would ring hollow.

“The issues that motivated me to bring this proceeding are being examined in the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion. The commissioner’s report will be handed down in December following a national examination of how antisemitism became so normalised in Australia.”

Cassuto added: “Ms Kostakidis can make her own accounting of her conduct. The Australian public can make theirs. I do not intend to spend another year taking Ms Kostakidis’ repugnant commentary from the dark corners of the internet and giving it a federal court platform in her pursuit of martyrdom. My job here is done.”

australia.title: NSW police seize 36 illegal ebikes on northern beaches that are now destined for the crusher
australia.snippet: Officers found one 14-year-old’s ebike was capable of hitting 90km/h. Owners have two weeks to appeal the seizure before the bikes will b...
australia.content:
Dozens of high-powered and illegal ebikes have been seized by police on Sydney’s northern beaches just weeks after the force was granted new powers to destroy dangerous bikes.

The operation was part of a coordinated push with the New South Wales government to ensure people only ride legal ebikes that have not been modified to reach high speeds.

One of the ebikes seized on Friday belonged to a 14-year-old boy from Warriewood. Police said it was capable of reaching speeds of more than 90km/h.

NSW police said they seized 36 “illegal ebikes”. The operation was launched on the northern beaches “following recent incidents of illegal, dangerous and reckless e-bike use”.

Assistant commissioner David Driver said police would be launching more operations across the state in coming weeks.

“Most ebike riders do the right thing and comply with the rules; however, police will enforce [the] new legislation if people ride non-compliant vehicles,” Driver said on Saturday.

In late August, NSW police were given new powers to destroy ebikes capable of exceeding the legal speed limit.

Owners of seized ebikes now have 14 days to let police know whether their bike was stolen and being used by someone else on Friday.

After that two-week window, the bikes will be “crushed”, the government says.

The legislation also allowed police to seize ebikes that do not cut power assistance at 25km/h, with non-compliant bikes to be removed from the streets.

The government invested in a number of “dyno units” – portable speed-testing devices – to measure an ebike’s power output.

The Transport for NSW secretary, Josh Murray, said one of the units was used on the northern beaches on Friday to inspect suspect ebikes.

“We can put an ebike on a machine and test its power and speed very quickly,” Driver said. “When they did that yesterday, the bike showed that just by clicking the throttle it could go over 40km/h.”

Ebikes have been hailed as a climate-friendly solution to city traffic congestion, transport emissions and even youth social media addiction, offering Australians a means to get more exercise and save money.

But they have come with a cost. NSW recorded 226 injuries related to ebikes in 2024. In the first seven months of 2025, that had already to surged to 233 injuries plus four deaths.

In NSW this year to date, 187 vehicle drivers, passengers and motorcyclists have died on the state’s roads. In 2025, the figure for the same period was 194.

Murray said most people were legally using ebikes but a small group ignoring the rules endangered other road users.

“We are serious about ebike safety and operations like this will continue by NSW police with support from Transport for NSW to ensure all road users are safe and complying with the state’s upgraded laws,” Murray said.

“Ebikes must behave like bicycles, not motorcycles. If your bike can operate like a motorcycle under throttle or go more than 25km/h while being powered, it is not legal to ride in public.

“Before you or your child jumps on an ebike, please make sure it’s road-legal, otherwise you risk losing the bike.”

australia.title: As China rises, Australia is increasingly enmeshed in the US war machine. Is the alliance still worth the risk?
australia.snippet: Australia is being exploited by an ally that could draw it, however unwillingly, into war with China, experts warn Get our new political ...
australia.content:
“Physical security matters,” said Kevin Rudd, at his axiomatic best before the National Press Club this week.

“Our first responsibility is to secure our people’s future in this most contested region of the world.”

Prime minister, to foreign minister, to ambassador, Rudd – on his self-declared, self-deprecatory “career trajectory towards infinitesimal demotion” – has an unparalleled perspective on Australia’s place in the world.

In a time of dramatic global upheaval, he argued, the nation’s security alliance with the United States was neither trivial nor sentimental.

“Our alliance with the United States remains a force multiplier for Australia’s defence needs.”

But, Rudd said, it did represent one of the seismic challenges Australia faced: countenancing “the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be in the future”.

Alliance with the US, he said, was necessary but not sufficient for the country’s long-term national security.

“We must also re-embrace national self-reliance to anticipate the full range of future uncertainties.” A Rudd sentence if ever one was said.

And the alliance, like any, carries risk.

Twice in a row, Rudd was asked whether Australia would even have a choice if the US were to become involved in a war with China over Taiwan, which Rudd judged a “one in three” chance in 2028 (the year of Taiwan’s next presidential election).

Or whether, in that scenario, Australian support would be automatically expected.

Both times Rudd declined to answer, even as he was asked directly whether – if US nuclear submarines were steaming from Australian ports, and US bombers taking off from Australian airfields, heading for Chinese sea and airspace – Australia could decline to be part of another American war.

“On Australian responses: I’ll engage in classic duck and weave,” Rudd said.

Growing enmeshment

This week, the Guardian published new data showing the US military and its defence industrial interests control, or have access to, more than 100 military bases across the Australian continent.

The enmeshment of the Australian military within the giant US war machine has hastened over recent years, and is set to grow even further.

US nuclear-capable bombers take off from Australian airfields on missions across the world – potentially carrying nuclear weapons (the US government won’t say, Australia won’t ask). From next year, nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines will port through HMAS Stirling off Perth.

The US remains Australia’s fundamental security ally, but it is also a country currently mired in what many international law experts say is an illegal, unprompted war, and one seen by many in Australia as a superpower in decline and increasingly unreliable.

The federal government maintains the US remains indispensable to Australian security. Marking 75 years of the Anzus Treaty this week, the deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the US “remains our closest ally and principal strategic partner”.

“For more than seven decades, the alliance has underpinned peace, stability and prosperity in our region and continues to contribute to the region’s strategic balance,” he said.

But a growing cohort of military strategists and geostrategic analysts argues Australia’s increasing enmeshment with the US military makes it less safe: that Australia is being exploited by an ally that could draw this country, however unwillingly, into war with China.

‘An automatic target’

David Vine, the author of Base Nation and The United States of War, told the Guardian the expansion of US military presence in Australia was of a scale unprecedented outside the conflicts in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq.

“What’s clear is that the US is preparing for war with China,” he said, “and for Australians, it’s worth thinking about whether they want to go to war with China, especially given Australia’s relative proximity.”

Australia did play – especially through Pine Gap – a significant role in the US global military system, Vine said, but the Australian military’s main role was as “a kind of auxiliary military force for the United States”.

Vine argued the current US-precipitated war in Iran had again demonstrated the “myth of the security umbrella” in hosting US bases.

“Hosting US bases turns a country into an automatic target; it makes host countries immediately complicit in anything and everything the US military might do, including waging war,” he said.

Instead of deterring potential adversaries, Vine said US military presence often escalated the risk of conflict.

“Building up US military power in China’s region and encircling China only encourages the Chinese military to respond in kind, to continue to build up its military power,” he said.

Vine argued that the breadth and scope of US military presence went far beyond any deterrent capability and instead demonstrated that the nation was preparing for a war that “frighteningly, too many people in the US military establishment assume is inevitable”.

“These are the same people who have been supporting a completely failed military strategy globally, who are making the world a far more dangerous place, and making it more likely that the United States and China and their respective allies will go to war.”

‘Every alliance is exploited’

During the presidency of Barack Obama, Dr Van Jackson served as a strategic adviser in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, when Australia took on a new geostrategic significance, part of that administration’s “pivot” to Asia.

“That pivot was about many things in relation to China, but specifically the geographic encirclement of China … in service of war fighting contingencies against China,” Jackson, an associate professor in international relations at the Victoria University of Wellington, told the Guardian.

“At the grand strategy level, it was about ensuring American primacy: global primacy is the principal means and ends of US foreign policy.”

Australia, as an ally, represents to the US an immensely useful piece of geography.

“Australia is this almost-perfect location to be distant enough from the immediate battle space in a Taiwan or an East China Sea scenario, but at the same time, close enough for power projection, for flowing forces, and to function as a kind of rear area base for recovery,” Jackson said.

Jackson noted the US-Australia alliance was often phrased in euphemism, around “mateship”, of shared values and of a commitment to democracy. Australia’s unswerving support for the US was part of that rhetoric too, he said, citing Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of war at the Pentagon, praising Australia for being “with us, even in our less-advisable wars”.

While Jackson believed “that romance” was authentically felt, it was secondary to the US’ interest in using Australia for “very exploitative reasons”.

“Every alliance is exploited … and geography is the purpose Australia serves,” he said.

Given the size of the US military – America’s military budget surpassed that of the next six largest defence budgets on earth combined (including two countries that were actively at war) – the contribution of American allies “in terms of boots on the ground, or the share of aircraft or of frigates, is always a drop in the bucket”, Jackson said.

“When military strategists in the Pentagon think about alliances it’s always about needing access to bases, ports, and airspace,” he said.

“It helps on the margins to have these almost-symbolic military contributions from allies, but it’s not decisive in any way, it doesn’t really ever shift the balance of power, it’s not the difference between victory and defeat: it’s about access.”

australia.title: Molly Ticehurst’s parents fought for 870 days to see her killer jailed. Their courage may help save other women
australia.snippet: The mother and childhood educator was murdered by her ex-partner in 2024. On Friday he was sentenced to 28 years in jail Get our breaking...
australia.content:
With his shock of white hair and tattoed arms, mine worker Tony Ticehurst seems the epitome of a hardened rural bloke.

But behind this exterior is a devoted and soft-hearted father, painfully articulate under the immense weight of grief.

It has been more than two years since the youngest of his three children, 28-year-old Molly, was murdered by her abusive ex-boyfriend in the central western NSW town of Forbes.

Daniel Billings was on bail when he broke into Molly’s bedroom and killed her in a frenzied stabbing attack just before midnight on 21 April 2024.

He was enraged because she had reported sexual assault allegations to police a fortnight earlier, after his campaign of threats, violence and abuse.

The charges of rape were ultimately dropped when Billings pleaded guilty to murder. On Friday he was sentenced to 28 years’ jail. He will serve at least 20 years, which will make him 49 when eligible for parole.

Molly, a bubbly young mum and childcare educator, had a close and warm relationship with her parents. After injury forced her dad to quit work as a coal colliery truck driver, she regularly helped him around the house, hanging out his washing on the Hills Hoist he could no longer reach.

Molly’s parents were separated. She was her mother Kate Shaw’s only child and “entire world”. Photos of them together show them in peals of laughter.

When Billings started threatening to break into Molly’s house and kill her after she ended their relationship in late 2023, her parents tried to protect her. They encouraged her to go to police and hoped she might bolster her security by making use of the NSW government’s Staying Home Leaving Violence initiative.

While this program failed to respond in time, her dad changed her locks and installed lengths of dowel in her window frames, while her mum slept over when she felt frightened.

When their worst fears were realised, the family found itself at the centre of the nation’s battle against domestic violence.

In the thick of the maelstrom, Tony encouraged calm.

“Let’s not think of him or have vengeance in our hearts,” he wrote online, on the eve of her funeral. “Instead, think of the good memories Molly gave us.”

Many of Forbes’ 6,000 residents gathered on a local football oval dotted with balloons for the funeral. Tony told those gathered of his immense pride.

“Molly didn’t have to leave us to grow her angel wings – they came with her as standard equipment,” he said. “Every parent would like to see their child change the world, but not at this cost.”

‘She matters’

The court case stalled for more than 500 days as Billings’ lawyers negotiated with prosecutors. Through two frigid country winters and a sweltering summer, Tony and Kate appeared at every court mention.

Behind the scenes, Molly’s tormented dad sometimes called the local state MP, Phil Donato, at night to seek comfort and counsel. The former police prosecutor often took the Ticehurst family’s concerns to the NSW government.

“That’s the fabric of these country communities. When people are doing it tough, the community rallies together,” Donato said after one delay.

“Molly was such a well-known and highly regarded young woman, loved by everyone who knew her and they were immensely disappointed with the system failing her.”

On 3 November 2025, Tony ran out of diplomacy. Shaken and teary, he approached reporters outside Forbes court after yet another deferral.

“It seems to me that in life, the system let Molly down and in death continues the same route,” he said. “Instead of getting closure, all we get is anxiety, sadness and heartache.”

Nine days later, they finally heard Billings admit his crime.

After the plea, Tony walked out into Victoria park under the soft spring sunshine to spontaneous applause from locals.

Many wore shirts bearing Molly’s face and two words, “She matters”.

The family came face-to-face with Billings in the NSW supreme court in Orange almost a year later, on 3 September.

As Billings took his place in an elevated dock in the middle of the room, he glanced only briefly at his victim’s parents.

He did not look at them again during a two-day sentencing, instead leaning to stare at the floor as details of his extreme violence were aired.

Tony told the court he envisaged Billings’ journey from Parkes to Forbes under the cover of darkness to murder his daughter. A phone video played to the hearing showed Billings cheerfully singing along to Johnny Cash’s The Man Comes Around while driving.

“I hope every night Molly’s screams keep you awake and the hairs on your arm stand up at the terror,” Tony told Billings, referencing the song lyrics.

Sadness, heartbreak and sleepless nights had become the norm for Kate, her victim impact statement said.

“Molly’s life was taken far too soon in a violent, malicious manner for no reason other than selfishness,” she said.

The courtroom, filled with about 50 relatives, friends and supporters of the Ticehurst family, was heavy with sadness. After more than 870 days, their bravery, patience and advocacy have come to something.

Their advocacy has ushered in tighter NSW bail laws and closer monitoring of those accused of domestic violence. It has raised awareness of the red flags for intimate-partner homicide along with the unique risks faced by rural women.

The family has called on the premier, Chris Minns, to release an investigation into her interactions with the Staying Home Leaving Violence scheme.

Although there is much more to do, including better funding for in-demand rural support services, Pia Birac, the deputy chief executive of Domestic Violence NSW, says Molly’s legacy will endure.

“Her story is a powerful reminder of what’s at stake when our systems fail to keep women safe,” she says. “It’s prompted national reflection, renewed scrutiny to responses to domestic and family violence.

“That’s due to the courage of her family.”

world.title: $15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwide
world.snippet: Her Horizon Fund seeks $100m to stop practice harming 230m women and girls globally Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against ...
world.content:
Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.

The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.

The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.

Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.

The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.

The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.

Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”

UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.

Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.

“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.

Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.

In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.

The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering a constitutional challenge to the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the new Child Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.

Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.

“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”

She added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”

Gibbs, who attended a Justice for Girls global gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.

“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.

“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”

FGM is the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.

A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately 44,000 deaths each year in the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.

world.title: Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdom
world.snippet: Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarch A traditional ...
world.content:
A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.

On Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.

However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.

The kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”

In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.

She also claimed that the royal family had been put under house arrest. Troops had “removed the royal guards without notice, and ... were deployed around the palace,” she said. “We cannot leave or receive people freely.”

Oyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son in a social media post on 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death.

“His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said.

Another contender had been Prince George Desmond-Kamurasi, who plays for the London amateur football club South East Dons. According to the committee, the goalkeeper had declined the offer of the throne because of his other responsibilities.

The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.

Andrew Mwenda, ⁠a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s ​family had not been able to produce a photo ​of the purported son, and declined to disclose ​details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed ​him if he were born to ‌a queen officially married ​to the king.

The prime minister ​called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said in a social media post.

“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.”

Edward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III.

Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda.

Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics.

In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored by the current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993.

The Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations of forgery and poisoning.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
world.snippet: Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’ Uganda is withdrawing f...
world.content:
Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.

Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”

The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.

When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”

The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.

At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”.

The Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know.”

The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by the head of the royal household, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.

The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”.

Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.

The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.

world.title: Babies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study finds
world.snippet: Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems Babies born to mother...
world.content:
Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.

Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.

More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.

Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town in South Africa, followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.

On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.

Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.

“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.

The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.

Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.

“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”

The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.

The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.

The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.

The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.

While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress has stagnated over the past two decades.

“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.

The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.

It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.

Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”

world.title: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia
world.snippet: US-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa The scourge of Somali...
world.content:
The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.

Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.

Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has mainland Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.

The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.

However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.

In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.

He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”

According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.

A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”

Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.

Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.

Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.

Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.

According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.

Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.

That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.

In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.

During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.

Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.

The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.

Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.

“What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.

“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.

“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”
